solution_full: Put $x=4\sin^{2}\theta$, increasing on $[0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$, so $x:0\to4$ corresponds to $\theta:0\to\frac{\pi}{2}$; $dx=8\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta$.

Wallis' formula (both exponents even, so a factor $\frac{\pi}{2}$): $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{6}\theta\cos^{2}\theta\,d\theta=\dfrac{(5\cdot3\cdot1)(1)}{8\cdot6\cdot4\cdot2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{15}{384}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{5\pi}{256}$.
So the integral is $512\cdot\dfrac{5\pi}{256}=10\pi=31.4159\ldots$, which is $31.42$ to two decimal places.
originality_note: New: an algebraic integral over [0,4] that turns into a mixed Wallis integral sin^6 cos^2 under x = 4 sin^2 theta (way 5). Closest known: int_0^4 (x+2)/sqrt(4x - x^2) dx and int_0^{2a} x^n sqrt(2ax - x^2) dx in textbooks. Different because: the power x^2 with the root gives a mixed-exponent Wallis integral with a large coefficient.

concept_use.Walli's theorem in Integration: After x = 4 sin^2 theta the integral is 512 int_0^{pi/2} sin^6 cos^2, evaluated by Wallis' formula.

stem_review: Read as a student: integrand real on [0,4]; quadrature gives 31.4159 = 10 pi. Answer 31.42, a positive decimal as planned. Changed: No change.
key_step: Substitute x = 4 sin^2 theta and apply Wallis to sin^6 cos^2.
justification: Routine chain: one substitution, one Wallis evaluation. Above 2021-P2-Q11 (L1) because the substitution must be chosen; L2.
